name: Essential AI Tools for the Workplace
objectives: Before you use AI at work, find your workplace AI policy and write down its three key rules, or three safe-default rules if there is none, with no customer or employee personal data going into AI tools
Given rough notes for a work message, write a clear work email with a chat assistant using a prompt with purpose, reader, key points and tone, with every fact checked and the email sounding like you

chapters.name: Chapter 1: The rules and the basic tools

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your employer's AI policy comes first
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and follow your workplace's rules for AI tools.
This lesson builds toward: Before you use AI at work, you will find your workplace AI policy and write down its three key rules, or three safe-default rules if there is none, with no customer or employee personal data going into AI tools.
Many employers have rules about AI tools: which tools are approved, what information can go into them, and when you must say you used AI. Breaking these rules can get you in trouble, even if you meant well.
Look in your employee handbook, intranet or IT pages, or ask your manager or IT: "Which AI tools are we allowed to use, and what information can I put in them?" Some employers provide a business version of a tool, such as Microsoft Copilot with a work account, that has more data protection than a personal free account.
If there is no policy, follow safe defaults: no customer or patient information, no employee personal data, no passwords, no confidential plans or financial numbers in personal AI accounts. Check every fact before sharing.
Step by step:
- Search your handbook or intranet for "AI".
- Ask your manager or IT which tools are approved.
- Ask what information is allowed.
- If there is no policy, use the safe defaults.
Words to know:
- AI policy: an employer's rules for using AI tools at work.
- Approved tool: a tool your employer allows for work.
- Confidential: information meant only for people inside the company.
Try it now: Find your workplace AI policy, or ask about it. Write down the three most important rules. If you are job seeking, write the three safe-default rules you will follow.
You can now find and follow the rules for AI tools at your workplace.

check.q: Where can you usually find your workplace AI policy?
options: In the handbook or intranet, or by asking your manager or IT
check.why: Policies are usually in the handbook or intranet, and your manager or IT can tell you.

check.q: Your workplace has no AI policy and you want help with a customer complaint reply. What do you do?
options: Paste the customer's name, address and order history
Use AI with any data you like
Leave the customer's personal details out and use a safe default
check.why: With no policy, the safe default is to keep customer and employee personal data out.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A chat assistant for everyday work writing
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn rough notes into a clear work message with a chat assistant.
This lesson builds toward: Given rough notes for a work message, you will write a clear work email with a chat assistant using a prompt with purpose, reader, key points and tone, with every fact checked and the email sounding like you.
Chat assistants such as ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini turn rough notes into clear writing. Use the one your workplace allows.
A good work prompt says the purpose, the reader, the key points and the tone: "Write a short email to my team. Purpose: the loading dock is closed Thursday for repairs. Use dock B instead. Deliveries arrive 7-11 am. Tone: clear and friendly. Under 100 words."
Then ask for changes ("shorter", "more formal", "add a bullet list"), check every fact, and make it sound like you before sending.
Step by step:
- Write your rough notes.
- Prompt with purpose, reader, key points and tone.
- Ask for one change at a time.
- Check names, dates, times and numbers.
- Edit to sound like you, then send.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type to ask an AI tool for something.
- Tone: how writing sounds: friendly, formal, firm.
Try it now: Write rough notes for a real or sample work message. Use a chat assistant to turn them into a clear email, ask for one change, and check every fact.
You can now turn rough notes into a clear work message with a chat assistant.

check.q: What does "for my manager, friendly tone" set in a prompt?
check.why: Naming the reader and the tone helps the AI write the right kind of message.

check.q: The AI's email draft says the meeting is Thursday, but your notes say Wednesday. What do you do?
options: Send it; the AI is probably right
Fix the day before you send it
check.why: You check every fact against your notes before sending.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: AI inside Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find and use the AI helper in the office apps you use, if your account has it.
This lesson builds toward: In the office apps you use, you will find and use the built-in AI helper, or an approved chat assistant if your account does not have one, using only non-confidential text in any tool your workplace has not approved.
Microsoft adds Copilot to apps like Word, Outlook, Excel, PowerPoint and Teams, and Google adds Gemini to Gmail, Docs, Sheets and Meet. Whether you have these depends on your employer's plan and settings.
Where you have them, the AI can work on what is already open: "Summarize this document", "Draft a reply to this email", "Suggest a formula for this column". Look for the AI icon or panel in the app, or ask IT how to turn it on.
If you do not have it, you can still copy non-confidential text into an approved chat assistant and paste the result back. Either way, you own the final version and you check it.
Step by step:
- Open Word, Outlook, Docs or Gmail with your work account.
- Look for the AI icon or panel, or ask IT.
- Ask it to summarize or draft from the open file.
- If not available, use an approved chat assistant with non-confidential text.
- Check and edit the result.
Words to know:
- Microsoft 365: Microsoft's set of work apps: Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams and more.
- Google Workspace: Google's set of work apps: Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Meet and more.
Try it now: Open a work document or email (or a sample one). Use the built-in AI helper if you have it, or an approved chat assistant if not, to draft a reply or a summary. Check it.
You can now use the AI helper in your office apps, or a safe alternative, to draft and summarize.

check.q: What is Copilot in Word or Outlook?
options: An AI helper built into Microsoft 365, on some plans
check.why: Copilot is built into Microsoft 365 apps, depending on the employer's plan and settings.

check.q: You do not see an AI icon in your office app. What do you do?
options: Install any AI extension you find
Ask IT, or use an approved chat assistant with non-confidential text
Paste confidential files into a personal AI account
check.why: IT can tell you what is available, and an approved assistant works with non-confidential text.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Summarizing documents and meetings
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a long document or meeting notes into key points and action items.
This lesson builds toward: Given a long document or meeting notes, you will summarize it into five key points and three action items with owners, checked against the original.
A summary saves everyone time. Ask for a specific shape: "Summarize this policy in five bullet points for a new hire, then list three action items." Or for meeting notes: "List decisions, action items with owners and due dates, and open questions."
Some meeting tools can transcribe and summarize meetings when your employer turns that on. Everyone in the meeting should know it is being recorded or transcribed; follow your workplace rules.
Summaries can leave out something important or get a detail wrong. Check the key facts against the original, especially numbers, dates, names and who agreed to do what.
Step by step:
- Paste or open the document (if allowed).
- Ask for bullets, decisions and action items with owners and dates.
- Compare key facts with the original.
- Fix anything missing or wrong before sharing.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version that keeps the main points.
- Action item: a task someone agreed to do, ideally with an owner and a due date.
- Transcribe: turn speech into written text.
Try it now: Take a long work document or meeting notes (or a public policy if job seeking). Ask AI for five bullets and three action items with owners, then check them against the original.
You can now summarize documents and meetings into clear points and action items, and check them.

options: A summary of the whole meeting
A task with an owner and a due date
check.why: Action items say who does what by when.

check.q: The AI's summary leaves out a deadline that is in the original document. What do you do?
options: Add the deadline after comparing with the original
Share the summary as it is
Ask for a longer summary and do not check it
check.why: Summaries can leave out details, so you compare with the original and fix it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Getting spreadsheet help from AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to write and explain a spreadsheet formula, then test it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a small spreadsheet, you will use AI to write and explain a formula, then test it, against an answer you worked out by hand.
Many workers lose time on spreadsheets. AI is a good tutor: "In Excel, how do I count how many rows in column B say 'Late'?" It might answer =COUNTIF(B:B,"Late") and explain each part.
Describe your columns instead of pasting confidential data: "Column A is date, B is status, C is hours." If your employer allows built-in AI in Excel or Sheets, you can ask it about the open file.
Always test a formula on a few rows where you know the answer. AI formulas can be close but wrong, for example counting the header row or using the wrong range.
Step by step:
- Describe your columns and what you want to know.
- Ask AI for a formula and an explanation.
- Paste the formula into your sheet.
- Test it on rows where you know the answer.
- Ask AI to fix it if it is wrong.
Words to know:
- Formula: an instruction in a spreadsheet cell that calculates something.
- COUNTIF: a formula that counts cells that match a condition.
- Range: a group of cells, like B2:B50.
Try it now: Make a small sheet with 10 rows of sample data. Ask AI for one formula (count, sum or average), paste it in and test it against an answer you work out by hand.
You can now get, understand and test spreadsheet formulas with AI help.

check.q: What is a range in a spreadsheet?
options: A group of cells, like B2:B50
check.why: A range is a group of cells that a formula works on.

check.q: The AI's COUNTIF formula gives 11, but you count 10 "Late" rows by hand. What do you do?
options: Check the range, for example whether it includes the header row, and fix it
check.why: A common mistake is the wrong range or counting the header, so you test and fix.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Checking AI work before you share it
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use a short checklist to review any AI output before it goes to others.
This lesson builds toward: Before you share any AI output, you will check it for facts, fit, safety and source, and take responsibility for the final version.
At work, your name is on what you share. Use a four-point check every time: Facts (numbers, names, dates, policies match the source), Fit (right tone and length for the reader), Safety (no confidential or personal data that should not be there), and Source (if it states a rule or a statistic, you know where it came from).
AI can make up details that sound right, called hallucinations. It can also copy bias, for example in a job description. Read it as if you were the person receiving it.
If your workplace asks you to say when you used AI, do it. Being open about how you work builds trust.
Step by step:
- Facts: check against the source.
- Fit: right tone and length for the reader.
- Safety: no data that should not be there.
- Source: know where any rule or number came from.
- Say you used AI if your workplace requires it.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Bias: an unfair slant for or against a group.
Try it now: Final task: complete your workplace AI task set: three policy rules, a clear email from notes, a five-bullet summary with action items, a tested spreadsheet formula, and a note of what you checked in each using Facts, Fit, Safety and Source.
You can now use workplace AI tools to get work done faster, safely and with your own careful check.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Policy rules No rules written, or rules that allow personal data in AI tools. Three key rules from the workplace AI policy, or three safe-default rules. Says where the policy is and who to ask about it. Clear email The email is unclear, or a fact is wrong. A clear email from rough notes, with facts checked against the notes. The learner asked for one change and made it sound like them. Summary and action items Fewer than five points, or action items without owners. Five bullet points and three action items with owners, checked against the original. Action items also have due dates, and a missing detail was found and added. Tested formula The formula was not tested or gives a wrong answer. A working formula tested against an answer worked out by hand. The learner can explain what each part of the formula does. Checks before sharing No note of what was checked. Each item has a note of the Facts, Fit, Safety and Source checks. The notes name a specific fix made after a check. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does the Safety check ask before you share AI work?
options: Whether it contains confidential or personal information that should not be shared
check.why: The Safety check makes sure nothing confidential or personal goes where it does not belong.

check.q: AI wrote a policy summary that quotes a rule. What do you do before sharing?
options: Check where the rule came from (Source) and that it is correct
check.why: The Source check confirms where any rule or number came from.
